nary_nodes.label: Group of Seven impacted Canadian identity
evidence: The Group of Seven was Canada's first internationally recognised national art movement, and they helped create a distinct, modern Canadian identity in the 1920s.

The painting by FH Varley is one of the most iconic works by The Group of Seven, a groundbreaking art collective who broke with the dominant tradition of European academic painting to create a uniquely Canadian style that revelled in the country's vast natural beauty.
What is it about their paintings that, for many, embody the Canadian spirit and identity?
The group's most celebrated works are "almost like what the Statue of Liberty is for the United States," says Katerina Atanassova, senior curator of Canadian art at The National Gallery of Canada.

Their most acclaimed paintings, which include Thomson's The Jack Pine, The West Wind and Harris's North Shore, Lake Superior, have become, for many, the national paintings of Canada – embodying the country's spirit.
Even if the Group of Seven weren't conscious of doing so, they "would have contributed to the circumstances around how Indigenous people were being perceived and treated", says LaVallee.
This was largely down to the way their art was used to "create this popular narrative of Canada" which was picturesque but "excluded the Indigenous populations", she says.
For today's outdoor-loving Canadians, the group's art is a celebration of the country's outstanding natural beauty.

So beloved are they that 7 July is now celebrated as Group of Seven Day.

nary_nodes.label: MacDonald and Harris visited exhibition
evidence: A turning point occurred when MacDonald and Harris visited a landmark exhibition of contemporary Scandinavian art in Buffalo, US, in 1913.

nary_nodes.label: Tom Thomson died
evidence: Thomson's death in 1917, at the age of only 40, turned him into a cultural legend

nary_nodes.label: Group of Seven first exhibition
evidence: One review of their first exhibition compared their work to "the contents of a drunkard's stomach".

nary_nodes.label: Group of Seven work selected for exhibition
evidence: The group's work was selected for the British Empire Exhibition, held at Wembley in 1924, where it received a rapturous response with the British press praising its "distinct Canadian character."

nary_nodes.label: PNIAI formed
evidence: a fact that led to the formation of another group of seven in the early 1970s, the Professional Native Indian Artists Incorporated (PNIAI).
Jackson Beardy, Eddy Cobiness, Alex Janvier, Norval Morrisseau, Daphne Odjig, Carl Ray and Joseph Sanchez first started meeting in Odjig's craft shop in Winnipeg.

nary_nodes.label: PNIAI activism and impact
evidence: Although they all had different styles and opinions, they wanted to band together to support other artists and challenge exclusionary practices and the narrow view of what "native" art actually was.

"We had no one to show our work, so we had to do it ourselves. We acknowledged and supported each other as artists when the world of fine art refused us entry… Together we broke down barriers that would have been so much more difficult faced alone," Odjig later said.
The PNIAI played a vital role in correcting that, and LaVallee credits her own position – as one of the senior management of the National Gallery of Canada – to their activism.

nary_nodes.label: Government implemented policies on Indigenous populations
evidence: The government's brutal policies, begun in the late 19th Century, had seen them forcibly removed to reservations or residential schools where their movement was restricted and their cultural practices suppressed.

nary_nodes.label: National Gallery displays art side-by-side
evidence: The National Gallery now displays Indigenous and non-Indigenous art side by side in the same galleries.

nary_nodes.label: Atanassova: Group of Seven works are like Statue of Liberty
evidence: The group's most celebrated works are "almost like what the Statue of Liberty is for the United States," says Katerina Atanassova, senior curator of Canadian art at The National Gallery of Canada.

nary_nodes.label: Atanassova: Thomson embodied ideal direct experience
evidence: "He embodied that ideal, that direct experience that every artist wants to have," Atanassova tells the BBC.

nary_nodes.label: Atanassova: Thomson inspired Group of Seven
evidence: It was Thomson who "started the images of the solitary tree", and inspired the future Group of Seven artists to see that the Canadian wilderness "can be viewed as modern and painted as modern", says Atanassova.

nary_nodes.label: Atanassova: Group of Seven goal was to follow Thomson
evidence: when the group officially formed in 1920, "the goal was defined that they ought to follow in his footsteps," says Atanassova.

nary_nodes.label: Atanassova: Group of Seven intention was emotional portrayal
evidence: Their intention "was not to portray what nature looked like, but how it made them feel, the emotional state created by the starry sky, the windswept pine or the barren coastal line on the north shore of Lake Superior."

nary_nodes.label: Atanassova: Foreign recognition made Group of Seven popular
evidence: Recognition abroad meant that it "suddenly became popular in Canada", explains Atanassova.

nary_nodes.label: Atanassova: Group of Seven excluded Indigenous population due to focus on untamed nature
evidence: The fact that this "distinct Canadian character" excluded the Indigenous population has led to criticism of the group in some quarters, although Atanassova feels that this is unfair.
"You don't see any signs of civilisation in [the Group of Seven's] paintings," she says.
They were "looking for untamed nature in the tradition of modern Scandinavian art", which meant that they also excluded any sign of industrialisation.

nary_nodes.label: Atanassova: Group of Seven art embodies raw connection with nature
evidence: It embodies, says Atanassova, "that raw connection with nature – and it's exactly the nature you see [in the paintings]. The lakes are the same, the skies are the same. It's an expression of your own experience. What you see and what you feel and what you live."

nary_nodes.label: Odjig: PNIAI supported each other and broke barriers
evidence: "We had no one to show our work, so we had to do it ourselves. We acknowledged and supported each other as artists when the world of fine art refused us entry… Together we broke down barriers that would have been so much more difficult faced alone," Odjig later said.

nary_nodes.label: LaVallee: PNIAI was first self-organised Indigenous arts advocacy group
evidence: "They were quite distinct in that they were the first self-organised Indigenous-artists-run arts advocacy group that was formally incorporated that ever existed in Canada," says Michelle LaVallee, Director of the Indigenous Ways and Decolonization Department and Curatorial Initiatives of the National Gallery of Canada.

nary_nodes.label: LaVallee: No Indigenous curators or staff at the time
evidence: "At that time, there were no Indigenous curators, no Indigenous people working in institutions," LaVallee tells the BBC.

nary_nodes.label: LaVallee: Indigenous art not held in same esteem as non-Indigenous art
evidence: "It really wasn't held in the same esteem as [work by their] non-Indigenous peers, even though it is the first and the most authentic art that can be and should be called Canadian," says LaVallee.

nary_nodes.label: LaVallee: PNIAI may not have appreciated 'Indian Group of Seven' name
evidence: Although the media soon dubbed them "the Indian Group of Seven", LaVallee isn't sure they would have appreciated the name.
"They were very intentional about what they called themselves," she says.
It was very important for them to have "Professional" and "Native Indian" present in the name of the group.

nary_nodes.label: LaVallee: Group of Seven and PNIAI have different approaches to land
evidence: While LaVallee herself likes the paintings of the Group of Seven, she points out that their approach to landscape is vastly different to the PNIAI.
"A lot of the PNIAI's works you would look at and not necessarily call it a landscape."
They are different ways of referencing the land".
It is art by "somebody from the land versus settlers coming and appreciating the land", she says.

nary_nodes.label: LaVallee: Group of Seven contributed to perception of Indigenous people
evidence: Even if the Group of Seven weren't conscious of doing so, they "would have contributed to the circumstances around how Indigenous people were being perceived and treated", says LaVallee.

nary_nodes.label: LaVallee: PNIAI activism led to her position
evidence: "For me to get to a place like that would not have happened had these earlier artists not fought for these types of rights and opportunities and created avenues of support and camaraderie between Indigenous peoples," she says.

nary_nodes.label: LaVallee: National Gallery display change not to erase histories
evidence: LaVallee emphasises that this is not meant to "erase or discredit any existing histories".

nary_nodes.label: LaVallee: First art and people of Canada were Indigenous
evidence: "Part of the change we're trying to assert is the idea that, yes, within Canada, it's very multicultural, but the first art of this land was Indigenous, and the first people of these lands were Indigenous, and that needs to be acknowledged and respected and recognised."
